influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/source: The Neoplatonism of Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus and Proclus: the ineffable One, procession and return, hierarchy and union beyond knowledge
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/christ: Apophatic (negative) theology, the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies, the threefold way of purification, illumination and union, and much of medieval mysticism
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/place/: Syria (probable home of the Dionysian author)
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/eviden: In 1895 Hugo Koch and Josef Stiglmayr independently showed that Divine Names 4.18–35 closely follows Proclus’s treatise On the Existence of Evils, proving that the Dionysian corpus dates from c. 500 and depends on late Neoplatonism. Augustine’s debt to Plotinus and Porphyry is explicit in his own writings.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/popula: Christian mysticism is pagan Neoplatonism with a thin Christian varnish, and the writings attributed to Dionysius, Paul’s convert in Athens, were a deliberate fraud that smuggled pagan philosophy into the church.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/whatHi: The dependence on Neoplatonism is beyond doubt, and the corpus is pseudonymous: it cannot be by the first-century Dionysius of Acts 17:34. Scholars such as Paul Rorem and Andrew Louth note, however, that pseudonymity was a recognised literary convention, and that the author deliberately reworked Proclus: he makes the Trinity, not an impersonal One, the source of all; he replaces theurgic rites with the church’s sacraments; and he grounds everything in the incarnation. Whether the result is ‘Christianised Neoplatonism’ or ‘Neoplatonised Christianity’ remains a matter of emphasis and confessional judgement.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/summar: Late Neoplatonism shaped Christian mystical theology through two main channels: Augustine in the West and the anonymous author writing as Dionysius the Areopagite c. 500. The borrowing is among the best documented in this atlas; its significance is still debated.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/story:
Neoplatonism was founded by Plotinus (204/5–270), whose Enneads were edited by his pupil Porphyry. It taught that all reality flows from a utterly simple and ineffable One, through Intellect and Soul, down to matter, and that the soul can return by purification and contemplation to a union beyond words. Later Neoplatonists — Iamblichus (c. 245–325) and Proclus (412–485), head of the Academy at Athens — added elaborate hierarchies of divine beings and theurgy, ritual acts thought to raise the soul to the gods. Porphyry also wrote a fifteen-book attack Against the Christians, later burned by imperial order.

Christians nonetheless found Neoplatonism congenial. Marius Victorinus, a famous Roman rhetor who converted c. 355, used Plotinus in his trinitarian writings. In Milan in 386 Augustine read translated ‘books of the Platonists’, almost certainly Plotinus and Porphyry, and described an ascent of the mind to ‘That Which Is’ (Confessions 7.17; 9.10, the vision at Ostia). In the East Gregory of Nyssa’s theme of the soul entering the ‘divine darkness’ on Sinai, though rooted in Exodus and Philo, shares the Neoplatonic language of a God beyond comprehension.

The decisive figure is the author who wrote c. 500, probably in Syria, under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul’s Athenian convert. His four treatises — The Divine Names, The Mystical Theology, The Celestial Hierarchy and The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy — and ten letters present a cosmos of ordered hierarchies through which divine light descends and by which creatures are lifted back to God, culminating in an ‘unknowing’ union beyond all affirmation and negation. The works are first cited by the anti-Chalcedonian Severus of Antioch and were debated at a colloquy in Constantinople in 532, where Hypatius of Ephesus doubted their authenticity. Their dependence on Proclus was proved only in 1895.

Apostolic authority gave the corpus enormous influence. John of Scythopolis annotated it c. 540, and Maximus the Confessor integrated it into a Christ-centred theology. In the West, Hilduin of Saint-Denis (c. 832) and John Scotus Eriugena (c. 862) translated it into Latin; the identification of Dionysius with Saint Denis of Paris inspired Abbot Suger’s light-filled Gothic choir at Saint-Denis (1144). Thomas Aquinas cites Dionysius some 1,700 times; Bonaventure, Meister Eckhart and the English Cloud of Unknowing all depend on him, and the ‘threefold way’ of purgation, illumination and union became a staple of spiritual direction. In the East, Gregory Palamas and the hesychasts, and in modern times Vladimir Lossky, drew on his apophatic theology.

Critics have pointed both to the authorship and to the content. Lorenzo Valla and Erasmus doubted that a disciple of Paul wrote the works. Martin Luther judged Dionysius ‘more a Platonist than a Christian’ (The Babylonian Captivity of the Church, 1520), and later Protestant writers saw the hierarchies as a pagan model of mediation that obscured Christ. Orthodox and Catholic theologians generally accept the pseudonymity but defend the substance as genuinely Christian, while acknowledging that its forms are Neoplatonic.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/howItH: Educated converts such as Marius Victorinus and Augustine read Plotinus and Porphyry in Latin translation and used them to think about God and the soul.
An anonymous Christian author c. 500 rewrote Proclus’s metaphysics in Christian terms and published under an apostolic name.
The apparent apostolic authority of ‘Dionysius’ secured acceptance by both Chalcedonians and anti-Chalcedonians.
Scholia by John of Scythopolis and the theology of Maximus the Confessor anchored the corpus in orthodoxy.
Latin translations from the ninth century carried it into Carolingian, scholastic and mystical theology in the West.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/exampl: Augustine’s ascent and the vision at Ostia (Confessions 7.17; 9.10).
Divine Names 4.18–35, a reworking of Proclus’s On the Existence of Evils.
The nine choirs of angels in three triads (Celestial Hierarchy 6–9), adopted in medieval art and Dante’s Paradiso.
The Mystical Theology’s ‘divine darkness’ and the fourteenth-century Cloud of Unknowing.
Abbot Suger’s Gothic rebuilding of Saint-Denis, inspired by Dionysian light theology.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/defend: Interpreted Dionysius christologically in the Ambigua and Mystagogy, making him central to Byzantine theology.
Translated the corpus into Latin c. 862 and built his Periphyseon on its scheme of procession and return.
Commented on the Divine Names and cited Dionysius as an authority throughout the Summa.
Presented Dionysian apophaticism as the heart of Eastern Orthodox mystical theology (1944).
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/critic: Questioned in the 1450s whether Paul’s Athenian convert could have written the corpus.
Called Dionysius ‘more a Platonist than a Christian’ and warned against his speculative mysticism (1520).
Treated the Dionysian corpus as a prime example of the paganising of Christian piety.
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/keptBy: Eastern Orthodox theology and hesychast spirituality
Oriental Orthodox churches, especially the Syriac tradition, where the corpus circulated early in translation
Contemplative movements across traditions that use apophatic prayer
influences/neoplatonism-mysticism/reject: Luther and much classical Protestant theology
Liberal Protestant historians who saw it as Hellenisation
Some modern evangelical critics of contemplative prayer
influences/midsummer-st-john/name: St John's Eve and midsummer fires
influences/midsummer-st-john/sourceCultu: Summer-solstice customs: bathing, bonfires, herbs and divination (later Slavic Kupala and Baltic Jāņi)
influences/midsummer-st-john/christianFo: The Nativity of John the Baptist (24 June) and the bonfires, bathing and herb-gathering of St John's Eve
influences/midsummer-st-john/evidenceNot: The feast's date is Christian in origin. It is calculated six months before Christmas from Luke 1:26–36, and Augustine connected it with John 3:30 ('He must increase, I must decrease'). Pre-Christian solstice customs attached to it are attested early. Augustine (Sermon 196.4) and Caesarius of Arles (Sermon 33.4) condemned pagan bathing on John's day, and canon 65 of the Council in Trullo (692) banned leaping over fires. The great midsummer bonfires, however, are first clearly described in the twelfth century (Johannes Beleth). Whether they continue pre-Christian solstice fires is likely but not proven.
influences/midsummer-st-john/popularClai: St John's Day is simply the pagan summer solstice festival, with its bonfires, renamed after John the Baptist.
influences/midsummer-st-john/whatHistori: Liturgists agree the date of 24 June derives from the date of Christmas, since Luke places John's birth six months before Jesus'. They also agree that Christian writers noticed the solar symbolism: John was born as the days begin to shorten, Christ as they lengthen. Late-antique bishops in North Africa and Gaul show that solstice bathing and festivities clung to the day. Ronald Hutton notes that the great medieval and early-modern bonfires are first documented by twelfth-century liturgists, who explained them as Christian symbols. Nineteenth-century folklorists such as Frazer read them as sun charms. So the adoption of a solstice festival-time is plausible, while specific rites are of uncertain antiquity.
influences/midsummer-st-john/summary: The feast of John the Baptist's birth on 24 June was set six months before Christmas, but it fell at midsummer. It drew solstice bathing, fires and herb customs which bishops from Augustine onward tried to suppress or reinterpret.
influences/midsummer-st-john/story:
John the Baptist is the only saint other than Mary whose birth, rather than death, the church celebrates. According to Luke, Elizabeth was six months pregnant at the Annunciation. Once Christmas was fixed on 25 December, John's nativity naturally fell on 24 June. Augustine saw meaning in the timing. John was born when the days begin to shorten and Christ when they begin to lengthen, fulfilling John's words, 'He must increase, but I must decrease' (John 3:30). Augustine was writing in North Africa around 400, and he also complained that on John's feast Christians imitated a 'pagan superstition' by bathing in the sea (Sermon 196.4).

Caesarius of Arles, in sixth-century Provence, likewise denounced people who bathed in springs, rivers and the sea at night on the feast of John (Sermon 33.4). Bishop Eligius of Noyon (d.660) is reported in his Life to have forbidden solstice dances and songs. The Council in Trullo (692), canon 65, banned the custom of leaping over fires lit before houses at the new moon. The canon does not name John's day, but it shows that fire rites troubled the church.

The classic midsummer bonfire is first clearly recorded in the twelfth century. The Paris liturgist Johannes Beleth (c.1160) and later William Durandus (1286) described bones and refuse burned on St John's Eve and wheels rolled downhill. They offered Christian explanations, such as recalling the burning of John's bones by the emperor Julian. In the late Middle Ages and early modern period, towns across Europe lit 'bonefires', gathered St John's wort and other herbs, and practised divination about love and harvest on that night.

In Eastern Europe the feast merged with the Slavic Kupala. The Russian Orthodox chronicle tradition and later church councils, such as the Stoglav Council of 1551, condemned bathing, fires and night-time games on Ivan Kupala. Latvian Jāņi and Lithuanian Joninės preserve the Baptist's name for national midsummer festivals. Some Protestant reformers abolished the saints' feasts, but bonfires often continued as civic customs. Puritans and Scottish kirk sessions disciplined participants in midsummer fires as superstitious.

Modern historians take a cautious middle position. The feast is Christian in origin and meaning, and its date is the result of the Christmas calculation. But it landed at the solstice and absorbed seasonal customs whose roots are probably pre-Christian. The bonfires and herb lore are documented mostly from medieval and early-modern sources. Frazer's idea that they are surviving 'sun charms' is a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated fact.
influences/midsummer-st-john/howItHappen: With Christmas on 25 December, Luke's six-month interval placed John's nativity on 24 June.
Augustine and others interpreted the solstice timing through John 3:30.
Popular solstice bathing and festivities attached themselves to the feast and were condemned by bishops (Augustine, Caesarius, Eligius).
Medieval towns developed St John's Eve bonfires, which liturgists explained in Christian terms (twelfth century onwards).
In Slavic and Baltic lands the feast fused with Kupala and Jāņi midsummer traditions.
influences/midsummer-st-john/examples/0: Augustine, Sermon 196.4: Christians bathing in the sea on John's feast.
influences/midsummer-st-john/examples/1: Caesarius of Arles, Sermon 33.4: night-time bathing in springs and rivers condemned.
influences/midsummer-st-john/examples/2: Council in Trullo (692), canon 65: ban on leaping over fires.
influences/midsummer-st-john/examples/3: Johannes Beleth (c.1160) on St John's Eve bonfires.
influences/midsummer-st-john/examples/4: Ivan Kupala in Russia and Ukraine; Jāņi in Latvia; Sankthansaften in Scandinavia.
influences/midsummer-st-john/defenders/0: Gave the solstice a Christian meaning: the forerunner decreases with the light as Christ increases (John 3:30).
influences/midsummer-st-john/defenders/1: Explained the bonfires and wheels as Christian symbols of John as 'a burning and shining lamp' (John 5:35).
influences/midsummer-st-john/critics/0/t: Condemned solstice sea-bathing on John's day as a pagan superstition.
influences/midsummer-st-john/critics/1/t: Preached against night-time bathing and pagan festivities on the feast of John in sixth-century Gaul.
influences/midsummer-st-john/critics/2/t: Condemned Kupala-night bonfires, bathing and revelry among Russian Orthodox believers.
influences/midsummer-st-john/keptBy/0: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches (Nativity of St John the Baptist, 24 June)
influences/midsummer-st-john/keptBy/1: Lutheran Scandinavia and the Baltic states as national midsummer holidays
influences/midsummer-st-john/rejectedBy/: Reformed and Puritan churches (saints' days and bonfires)
Many evangelical and Free Churches, which keep no saints' days
influences/midsummer-st-john/calendar/ch: Nativity of John the Baptist; St John's Eve (23 June)
